title: Lisbon to Barcelona by Train: A Two-Week Iberian Rail Route
metaDescription: A two-week Portugal and Spain rail itinerary from Lisbon to Barcelona — routes, booking, high-speed vs regional trains, and where to stop.
excerpt: Spain has one of the best high-speed networks in the world. Portugal has the slower, prettier trains. Together they make an excellent two weeks.
author: Trypinn Team
content:
Spain built one of the world's largest high-speed rail networks, which means the country is crossable in hours rather than days and the trains are genuinely fast — Madrid to Seville in around two and a half hours, Madrid to Barcelona in under three.

Portugal's network is slower and more scenic. Together, they make a two-week route that requires no car, no internal flights and very little planning beyond booking the right tickets at the right time.

## The Route

**Lisbon — 3 nights**

Hilly, faded, and one of Europe's most likeable cities. Alfama's lanes, the Tram 28 route (walk it instead, the tram is crowded), Belém for the monastery and the original pastéis, the LX Factory, and a viewpoint at sunset with a drink.

Day trip to **Sintra** — palaces in a forested hill range, 40 minutes by train. Go early; it gets extremely busy by mid-morning.

**Porto — 3 nights**

Train from Lisbon, roughly three hours on the Alfa Pendular.

Porto is the more atmospheric of the two cities — steep, tiled, and built around the Douro. The Ribeira waterfront, the Livraria Lello, São Bento station's tile panels, and the port houses across the river in Vila Nova de Gaia.

**The Douro Valley** is the day trip, and it is one of the great railway journeys in Europe — the line follows the river closely through terraced vineyards. Take the train to Pinhão and back; this is worth building the trip around.

![Portugal travel](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1504019347908-b45f9b0b8dd5?fm=webp&w=1200&q=60)

**Salamanca or Madrid — the crossing**

The Portugal–Spain rail connection is the weak link in an otherwise excellent network. Direct services are limited and journey times are long.

Two practical options:

- **Bus to Salamanca or Madrid**, which is faster than the train on this leg and perfectly comfortable
- **Overnight or a connection via Vigo and Galicia**, if you want to add northern Spain

**Salamanca** is worth a stop in its own right — a golden sandstone university city with one of the most beautiful squares in Spain.

**Madrid — 3 nights**

The Prado, the Reina Sofía, the Retiro, and a food culture that runs from the markets to late-night tapas. Madrid is a city for walking and eating rather than sightseeing checklists.

Day trips by high-speed rail: **Toledo** in 33 minutes, **Segovia** in under 30, **Córdoba** in under two hours. This is the real advantage of Spanish rail — cities that would be full-day excursions elsewhere become easy half-days.

**Seville and Andalusia — 3 nights**

Madrid to Seville is around two and a half hours.

Seville: the Alcázar, the cathedral and Giralda, Santa Cruz, Triana, and flamenco in a small venue rather than a tourist show. **Book the Alcázar in advance** — it sells out.

From Seville, **Córdoba** (45 minutes) for the Mezquita, and **Granada** (around three hours) for the Alhambra. The Alhambra requires **timed tickets booked weeks ahead** and is the most common "we could not get in" disappointment in Spain.

![Portugal travel](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1495562569060-2eec283d3391?fm=webp&w=1200&q=60)

**Valencia — 2 nights**

Seville or Madrid to Valencia by high-speed rail.

Valencia is the under-visited Spanish city: a beach, the City of Arts and Sciences, a riverbed converted into a nine-kilometre park, the best paella in the country (it is from here, and Valencians are firm about what belongs in it), and a compact old town.

**Barcelona — 3 nights**

Valencia to Barcelona in around three hours.

Gaudí — Sagrada Família, Park Güell, Casa Batlló, all requiring **advance timed tickets** — the Gothic Quarter, the Boqueria, Montjuïc, and the beach.

Note that Barcelona is actively managing tourism pressure, including phasing out short-term rental licences, so book accommodation earlier than you might expect and consider staying slightly outside the centre.

## Booking the Trains

**Spain**
- **Renfe** operates the high-speed AVE network, with competitors Ouigo and Iryo on some routes, which has pushed prices down significantly
- **Book 30 to 60 days ahead** for the cheapest fares. Prices rise steeply close to departure
- Tickets are released a few months in advance; there is no advantage to booking earlier than that
- Seat reservations are compulsory on high-speed services

**Portugal**
- **CP** operates the network. The Alfa Pendular is the fastest service; the Intercidades is slower and cheaper
- Book the Lisbon–Porto route ahead in summer
- Regional trains do not require reservations

**Passes**
A rail pass rarely beats point-to-point tickets on this route, because Spanish high-speed services require paid reservations on top of the pass, and advance-purchase fares are often cheaper than the reservation fee alone. Price both before assuming.

## When to Go

- **April to June** — the best window. Warm, green, and before the summer heat
- **September to October** — equally good, with warm seas
- **July and August** — very hot in Madrid, Seville and Córdoba, routinely above 38°C. Andalusia in August is genuinely difficult
- **November to March** — mild on the coast, cold inland, very few visitors, and cheap

## What It Costs

- **Budget** — $60–85 a day
- **Mid-range** — $120–180
- **Comfortable** — $250–400

Portugal is meaningfully cheaper than Spain. Rail costs across the whole route, booked in advance, are modest — frequently less than a fortnight's car hire and fuel would be.

## Variations

**Add northern Spain** — from Madrid, head north to **San Sebastián** for the food, **Bilbao** for the Guggenheim, and **Santiago de Compostela**. This is the best food region in Spain and the least hot in summer.

**Portugal only** — Lisbon, Sintra, Porto, the Douro, Coimbra and the Algarve, over ten days.

**Andalusia only** — Seville, Córdoba, Granada, Ronda and Cádiz, over ten days, which is a richer trip than trying to cover the whole peninsula.

## The Practical Advantages of Doing This by Rail

You arrive in city centres rather than airports. You do not park, navigate or pay tolls. You can drink wine at lunch. The journeys are part of the trip rather than an interruption to it — and on the Douro line and the approach to Barcelona along the coast, they are among the best parts.

The one thing to get right in advance is the bookings: high-speed fares, the Alhambra, the Alcázar and the Gaudí sites all need to be locked in weeks ahead, and they are what fix the shape of the itinerary. Settling those first, in one shared plan, and letting the flexible days arrange themselves around them is the right order of operations — **Trypinn** keeps the fixed points and the loose days visible to everyone in the group.
